AM4F-01.note: 14 = 10+4 with both signs dropped, -6 = -10+4, 6 = 10-4. Standard sign-error family.

AM4F-02.note: 9 = stopping at f(2); -7 = f(g(2)) (order reversed); -2 = g(2). Every wrong path is represented.

AM4F-06.solved: Right 3 replaces x with x-3; down 2 subtracts 2. y = f(x-3) - 2.
AM4F-06.note: All four sign combinations present, so the option set alone decides nothing.

AM4F-07.solved: Undefined where the denominator vanishes: 2x + 7 = 0, x = -7/2.
AM4F-07.note: Reciprocal/sign family (2/7, -2/7, 7/2). 7/2 is the likely wrong pick; the two 2/7 options are weaker.

AM4F-08.note: 1/3 punishes answering r instead of r^3 (what the stem actually asks); 27 and 3 are the reciprocal reads.

AM4F-09.note: Base and exponent-divisor swapped across the three wrong options.

AM4F-10.note: 'Total change' is slightly loose wording for net change. f dips to about -3.08 near x=1.155, so total VARIATION is about 51.16 - not an option, so the item stays exclusive, but 'net change' would be the cleaner stem. 48 = f(4) alone; 63 = 64-1 (the -4x dropped); 17 is the weakest option.

AM4F-11.note: 8 = f(1), 0 = using the wrong branch at both steps. 22 does not map cleanly to any wrong path I can construct - the weakest option in the set.

AM4F-12.solved: Axis of symmetry x = 12/4 = 3; the partner of x=1 is 2(3) - 1 = 5. Check: f(1) = -3, f(5) = 50-60+7 = -3.
AM4F-12.note: 3 = the axis itself (a very live wrong pick); -1 and -5 cover the reflection-through-origin errors.

AM4F-13.note: 0 = forgetting the -5 (3x+4=4); 5/3 = 3x+4=9; 7 = the radical's value rather than x.

AM4F-14.note: Full sign cross-product of (+-3, -10/8); 8 = f(3), so the sign-of-x error lands somewhere real.

AM4F-15.solved: Equal degrees, so the limit is the ratio of leading coefficients: 6/2 = 3.
AM4F-15.note: 1/3 = inverted ratio; 6/5 = wrong pair of coefficients; 0 = the lower-degree-numerator reflex.

AM4F-17.note: -14 = f(-2)+g(-2) (subtraction dropped); -2 = f(-2) alone; -10 = the sign-flip of the answer.

AM4F-18.solved: After the first hour, 2 h 25 min remain = 3 additional hours-or-parts at $3 = $9.
AM4F-18.note: 14 = the full charge 5+9, and the stem's 'for the time after the first hour' is the only thing keeping a careless student off it - that phrase is load-bearing and worded clearly enough. 6 = forgetting to round the partial hour up. The only non-function item in an otherwise function-themed batch.

AM4F-19.note: 1.875 = the answer to the question the stem does NOT ask (y at x=6, z=4) - a good trap given the stem deliberately asks only for k. 45 = k with z^2 misplaced.

AM4F-20.solved: Minimum = 11 - b^2/4 = 2, so b^2 = 36, b = +-6; b negative gives -6.
AM4F-20.note: 6 punishes ignoring 'b is a negative constant'; +-3 cover the halving slip. Clean.

AM4F-21.note: 12.5 is exactly h^-1(9) for the reversed composition g(f(x)) = (2x-1)/4 + 3 - the intended order trap, and a strong one. 9.5 = h(9); 5 = f^-1(9).

AM4F-22.note: The t=12 margin is only 9.15 on ~12,600 (0.07%). That is the item's whole point and A=12 is the trap, but it also means a student who rounds 1.08^12 to 2.52 gets a dead tie at 12,600 and must know that a tie is not 'more'. Defensible as written - the inequality is strict - but it is knife-edge enough that a calculator carrying two decimals can mislead. Flagging, not objecting.

AM4F-23.solved: Need 1/(x-6) - 2 >= 0 with x != 6. Only x > 6 can work; then 1 >= 2(x-6), x <= 6.5. So 6 < x <= 6.5.
AM4F-23.note: All four options are the same two numbers with the four endpoint combinations, so nothing is guessable from the option set; both endpoints have to be reasoned separately (one from the pole, one from the radicand). Genuinely two ideas interacting.

AM4F-24.solved: 3x - 9 = +-15 gives x = 8 or x = -2; greatest is 8.
AM4F-24.note: -2 is the other genuine root and punishes skipping 'greatest'; 24 = 15+9 without dividing; 2 = (15-9)/3.

AM4F-26.solved: (x-5)(x+2)/(x-5) = x + 2 for x != 5, so the hole sits at (5, 7).
AM4F-26.note: (5,3) uses the wrong factor's value; (-2,0) is the zero of the numerator, the other tempting 'special point'.

AM4F-27.note: 11 = a(3), the off-by-one. 37 and -2 do not correspond to any wrong recursion I can reconstruct; both are weak fillers.

AM4F-28.note: 60 = truncating to 2 whole halvings, the main trap; 96 and 182 cover linear-decay reads. Shares the exponential-model idea with AM4F-09 but the task (evaluate vs. select a model) is different enough not to be a duplicate.
